title: The Iran Cease-Fire Was Doomed to Fail
gist: Two Chatham House Middle East analysts argue the June 2026 US-Iran memorandum collapsed because transactional diplomacy postpones the contested issues instead of resolving them, and that the region is now replicating the pre-1914 dynamic of loose blocs, personal diplomacy and rearmament. The immediate market-relevant risk they flag is a simultaneous closure of the Strait of Hormuz by Iran and the Red Sea gateway by the Houthis, which they say would hit the global economy harder than any earlier phase of the 2026 fighting.

insights.claim: The June 2026 US-Iran memorandum of understanding — designed to halt fighting, open the Strait of Hormuz and create a 60-day negotiating window — has fallen apart, with both sides launching missiles and drones again and commerce through the strait shut down.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Hormuz is closed again as of late July 2026 — tanker rates, war-risk insurance and crude term structure should be priced off a live blockade, not a ceasefire.
insights.quote: Iran and the United States are back to launching missiles and drones at each other and have shut down commerce through the strait
insights.locator: The memorandum of understanding that the United States and Iran signed in June

insights.claim: The memorandum's failure was structurally predictable because it postponed resolution of the most contested issues between Washington and Tehran — the same formula Trump applied in Gaza.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Treat any future Trump-brokered Middle East deal that defers core issues as a pause with a short half-life, not a regime change in risk.
insights.quote: The agreement postponed the resolution of the most contested issues between the two adversaries—a formula that U.S. President Donald Trump favors
insights.locator: The memorandum’s failure should come as no surprise

insights.claim: If Israel concludes negotiations are over, or believes Iran is rebuilding missile capabilities, restoring proxy networks or returning to prohibited nuclear activity, it could re-enter the fight — making Israeli threat perception, not US-Iran talks, the operative escalation trigger.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Monitor Israeli intelligence signalling on Iranian missile reconstitution as the leading indicator for the next strike round.
insights.locator: IN TATTERS

themes.theme: Transactionalism as a doctrine and its limits

insights.claim: Transactional diplomacy rests on standalone bargains built around personal ties between leaders rather than institutional frameworks, and functions as instruments for managing present tensions rather than steps toward resolution — 'the geopolitical equivalent of a quick buck'.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: A test for deal durability: if an agreement has no institutional carrier beyond a leader relationship, assume it does not survive leadership or incentive change.
insights.quote: They are the geopolitical equivalent of a quick buck.
insights.locator: BARGAIN HUNTERS

insights.claim: Conflict management must not be conflated with conflict resolution: discrete deals fail when they substitute for institution building and tough political compromise, and a cease-fire without sustained diplomacy becomes a pause that warring parties use to prepare for the next round.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Do not de-risk portfolios on cease-fire headlines absent a follow-on political process — the base case is rearmament during the pause.
insights.quote: Unless a cease-fire is followed by sustained diplomacy, it risks becoming a mere pause that warring parties use to prepare for the next round.
insights.locator: There is nothing inherently wrong with a limited diplomatic bargain

insights.claim: The regional security dilemma is that Tehran's nuclear programme, missile arsenal and network of armed partners are defensive from Iran's perspective but intolerable from Israel's and Washington's, so the Iran war will keep flaring until a larger political process alters that dynamic.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Structural, not episodic, conflict risk in the Gulf — build a persistent geopolitical premium into energy and shipping assumptions.
insights.quote: Unless a larger political process begins to alter that dynamic, the Iran war will continue to flare into life.
insights.locator: At its core, the regional security dilemma

insights.claim: Middle East conflicts are so interconnected that pressure applied in one arena produces instability in another, so unresolved disputes cascade across the region rather than staying contained.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Model regional exposure as correlated: a Gaza, Yemen or Lebanon shock should be assumed to transmit to Gulf energy infrastructure.
insights.locator: The dangers of transactionalism are especially pronounced

insights.claim: The authors argue the present moment resembles the pre-World War I breakdown of the Concert of Europe, when ambiguous commitments, aversion to consultation, reliance on personal diplomacy and shortsightedness produced global catastrophe.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: The historical base rate for this configuration is systemic war, not muddling through — argues for fatter tail hedges than consensus.
insights.quote: the current moment resembles the lead-up to World War I, when ambiguous commitments, an aversion to consultation, a reliance on personal diplomacy, and shortsightedness produced a global catastrophe
insights.locator: THE WAR TO END ALL WARS

insights.claim: Citing historian Paul Schroeder, the authors argue the 1815 Concert of Europe worked because signatories saw themselves as custodians of the order rather than merely competitors within it, forgoing available gains to maintain stability and meeting to defuse tensions before they became crises.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: A diagnostic for order stability: watch whether major powers still absorb costs to maintain the system, or have shifted to pure opportunism.
insights.quote: the signatories saw themselves as custodians of the order, not just as competitors within it
insights.locator: As the historian Paul Schroeder has argued

insights.claim: The nineteenth-century concert eroded because nationalism, German and Italian unification and imperial competition changed how states understood their interests, leading them to treat disputes as chances to defend status, test others' credibility or seize advantage — leaving fewer tools to contain crises.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: The mechanism to watch today is credibility-testing behaviour replacing interest-based bargaining — it removes crisis off-ramps.
insights.locator: The system worked well for decades but began to erode

insights.claim: In 1914 the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente were loose arrangements rather than integrated values-based partnerships — Italy switched sides in 1915 — and suspicion that allies would not honour commitments drove rapid mobilisation that crowded out diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Loose, transactional coalitions are escalation accelerants, not stabilisers — relevant to how today's Middle East blocs behave under stress.
insights.quote: These were not closely integrated partnerships based on shared values but loose arrangements; Italy’s decision to switch sides in 1915 is a case in point.
insights.locator: The Triple Alliance brought together

insights.claim: German backing for Austria-Hungary in 1914 rested on the Schlieffen Plan's promise of rapid victory, so Vienna issued a harsh ultimatum to Serbia expecting a limited conflict — an illustration that transactional logic plus tunnel vision causes systematic misjudgement of escalation.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Actors who expect quick wins take bigger risks — assume Israeli, Iranian and US planners are similarly underestimating escalation length.
insights.locator: Tunnel vision led European leaders to misjudge

insights.claim: Narrow bargains have become more attractive because of weakening multilateral institutions, US retrenchment after Iraq and Afghanistan, declining confidence in large diplomatic projects such as the 1993 Oslo process and the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement, intensifying great-power competition, and the growing autonomy of regional powers.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: A checklist of structural drivers — none reversing soon, so expect a durable regime of short-dated, low-credibility international agreements.
insights.locator: BUYER’S REMORSE

insights.claim: Domestic politics reinforces transactionalism because voters reward leaders for achieving quick wins rather than long-term planning.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: The incentive is structural, not personal — the pattern outlives any single administration.
insights.quote: voters reward leaders for achieving quick wins, not long-term planning
insights.locator: These trends are reinforced at the domestic level

insights.claim: Trump treats long-standing alliances as negotiable arrangements judged by immediate benefit and relies on a small circle with little diplomatic background plus personal ties with foreign leaders to make deals.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Alliance-contingent assets (allied defence programmes, base-hosting economies) carry policy-reversal risk tied to a handful of personal relationships.
insights.quote: He treats long-standing alliances as negotiable arrangements and evaluates them based on their immediate benefit.
insights.locator: Nowhere is this clearer than in Washington

insights.claim: Trump's personal relationships with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Syrian leader Ahmed al-Shara drove a rapid 2025 reversal of US Syria policy: recognition of Shara's government, lifting of sanctions and removal of other barriers to reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Syria reconstruction exposure exists but rests on personal-relationship policy that could reverse as fast as it was granted.
insights.locator: Indeed, it was his personal relationships

insights.claim: Trump's May 2025 Gulf trip raised hundreds of billions of dollars in arms deals, aviation orders, technology transfers and promises to invest in American companies, while members of the Trump family simultaneously enriched themselves through cryptocurrency and real estate deals with firms tied to Gulf royals.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Quantifies the Gulf-to-US capital and order pipeline while flagging the influence-purchase channel — headline risk for both the deals and the counterparties.
insights.quote: a trip that raised hundreds of billions of dollars in arms deals, aviation orders, technology transfers, and other promises to invest in American companies
insights.locator: In May 2025, Trump visited the Gulf

insights.claim: Gulf leaders mistook access to Trump for influence over US policy, treated commercial ties as a substitute for security guarantees, and weakened their collective bargaining position by competing with one another for Washington's favour.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Gulf sovereigns' US investment commitments have bought less protection than assumed — their security risk premium is understated.
insights.quote: Gulf leaders mistook access to Trump for influence over U.S. policy.
insights.locator: At first, Gulf leaders took delight

insights.claim: Israel's strike on a residence in Qatar aimed at Hamas officials attending a US-backed negotiation demonstrated that Doha's transactional access to the White House gave it no leverage when it mattered, since it could neither prevent the attack nor influence Washington's closest regional partner.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Concrete precedent that Gulf hosting of US assets does not confer immunity — relevant to Qatari and UAE asset risk pricing.
insights.locator: Just a few months after Trump’s trip to the Gulf

insights.claim: Gulf leaders lobbied the Trump administration for months against military action, yet in February 2026 the United States and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran anyway.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Gulf lobbying has near-zero predictive value for US military action — do not treat Gulf reassurance as a de-escalation signal.
insights.locator: The limits of the Gulf’s sway became even clearer

insights.claim: Iran's retaliation hit US bases, energy infrastructure and hotels in the Gulf and blocked the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting shipping, driving up insurance premiums, delaying exports and reducing revenue flows across the region, with recovery expected to take years for some Gulf countries.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Multi-year damage to Gulf hydrocarbon logistics and tourism cash flows, plus a structurally higher marine insurance cost base.
insights.quote: Tehran also blocked the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting shipping, driving up insurance premiums, delaying exports, and reducing revenue flows across the region.
insights.locator: In response to the strikes, Iran attacked U.S. bases

insights.claim: The authors' counterfactual is that in early 2025 Gulf states should have pooled leverage to secure an institutionalised framework — consultation before major US military action, explicit territorial defence commitments, airspace rules and integrated missile and maritime defence — which would have raised the cost of war and reduced their exposure when deterrence failed.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: If Gulf states now pursue this, expect large integrated air and maritime defence procurement programmes as the investable expression.
insights.locator: A better approach in early 2025 would have been

insights.claim: Starting in 2020 several Arab states abandoned their decades-long promise to normalise with Israel only after Israeli withdrawal from Palestinian territories, trading normalisation for arms, trade benefits and security cooperation — with Morocco specifically obtaining US recognition of its sovereignty over Western Sahara.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Sets the template and price list for future normalisation deals — watch what a Saudi deal would extract.
insights.locator: LOSING STREAK

insights.claim: The October 7, 2023 Hamas attack was intended at least in part to prevent Saudi Arabia from joining the Abraham Accords, and it set off three years of regional war — making transactionalism in that case not merely hollow but dangerous.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Normalisation announcements are themselves escalation catalysts — treat any Saudi-Israel deal headline as a spoiler-attack risk event.
insights.quote: The attack was intended, at least in part, to prevent Saudi Arabia from joining the accords. In this case, transactionalism was not only hollow but also dangerous.
insights.locator: As Saudi Arabia contemplated its own normalization deal

insights.claim: Since the October 2025 Gaza cease-fire large-scale combat has mostly subsided, but Hamas remains armed, over 800 Palestinians have been killed, reconstruction has not started in earnest, and Israel still controls 70 percent of the enclave.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Hard metrics showing the Gaza cease-fire is a frozen occupation, not a settlement — Gaza reconstruction plays remain unfundable.
insights.quote: Hamas is still armed, over 800 Palestinians have been killed, reconstruction hasn’t started in earnest, and Israel remains in control of 70 percent of the enclave
insights.locator: Since the October 2025 cease-fire in Gaza

insights.claim: Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan has stalled as Washington's attention shifted elsewhere, and what attention the territory receives takes the form of outlandish development and tourism plans rather than processes addressing governance and reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Discount headline Gaza development or tourism schemes — the political preconditions are absent.
insights.locator: Palestinians are still suffering from the consequences

insights.claim: On July 13, 2026 the Houthis and Saudi Arabia traded strikes, breaking a cease-fire in place since 2022, and on July 20 the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Dated escalation on a second front — Saudi export and import logistics on the Red Sea coast are now directly threatened.
insights.quote: on July 13, the Houthis and Saudi Arabia traded strikes, breaking a cease-fire that had been in place since 2022. And on July 20, the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.
insights.locator: The Houthis, Iran’s ally in Yemen

insights.claim: If the Houthis shut the gateway to the Red Sea while Iran blocks the Strait of Hormuz, the consequences for the global economy would be worse than anything that occurred during earlier phases of the 2026 fighting.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: The single highest-impact tradeable scenario in the piece: simultaneous Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb closure — long tanker rates, energy, insurance; short import-dependent Asian and European industrials.
insights.quote: If the group escalates and shuts down the gateway to the Red Sea while Iran blocks the Strait of Hormuz, the consequences for the global economy could be worse than what occurred during earlier phases of fighting this year.
insights.locator: If the group escalates and shuts down the gateway

insights.claim: Regional blocs are hardening: Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are tightening coordination while Israel and the United Arab Emirates strengthen their own partnership, arrangements more fluid than 1914's alliances but capable of producing the same security dilemma over time.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: A concrete map of the emerging Middle East bloc structure — use it to anticipate arms-transfer flows and diplomatic alignment.
insights.quote: Today, Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey are tightening their coordination, while Israel and the United Arab Emirates are strengthening their own partnership.
insights.locator: Blocs are already hardening in response to the bloodshed

insights.claim: Gulf governments are rearming using Turkish and Ukrainian missile and drone expertise, which may improve national defence but could also spur Iran to accelerate its own build-up, and without military hotlines, exercise notification and rules for missiles and unmanned systems this rearmament raises the risk of a major regional war.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Turkish and Ukrainian defence exporters are the direct beneficiaries of Gulf rearmament, while the arms race itself raises the regional risk premium.
insights.quote: Gulf governments are also rearming and drawing on Turkish and Ukrainian missile and drone expertise.
insights.locator: Gulf governments are also rearming

insights.claim: The authors warn that without a wider peace process the Middle East may enter a state of near-permanent conflict, and that the past three years' fighting could set the stage for a worse war in the coming decade much as the 1912-13 Balkan Wars preceded World War I.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Frames the base case as chronic regional conflict rather than mean reversion — a permanent bid under defence, energy security and freight risk.
insights.quote: it may enter a state of near permanent conflict—a condition that no country can afford
insights.locator: Still, such a framework may seem distant

themes.theme: What a durable settlement would require

insights.claim: The authors' contrarian claim is that a larger deal may paradoxically be easier to secure than a narrow one, because a narrow bargain asks all parties to surrender leverage without addressing what drove them to war, whereas a broad framework can address every party's underlying security concerns at once.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: If negotiations restart, breadth rather than modesty is the signal of durability — a comprehensive framework announcement would be the genuine de-risking event.
insights.quote: A larger deal may, paradoxically, be easier to secure.
insights.locator: But a larger deal may, paradoxically, be easier to secure

insights.claim: A durable Iran settlement would pair sanctions relief with verifiable concessions on the nuclear programme and enriched-uranium stockpile, credible US and Israeli guarantees against renewed attacks, an enforceable framework for freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, and eventual Iran-Gulf nonaggression and noninterference understandings.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: A concrete term sheet to score any future deal against — sanctions relief without navigation enforcement is not a Hormuz de-risking event.
insights.locator: A more durable political settlement would see Iran receive sanctions relief

insights.claim: The proposed architecture is a Middle East-wide security dialogue modelled on the 1975 Helsinki Accords, with IAEA verification of nuclear provisions, phased sanctions relief overseen by the United States, European partners and the UN, and Oman, Qatar and Pakistan acting as regional mediators.
insights.speaker: Neil Quilliam
insights.so_what: Names the institutional vehicles and mediators to watch; activity from Oman, Qatar or Pakistan is the early tell that a broader process is forming.
insights.locator: Any bilateral agreement between the United States and Iran
